It's not the AI warning us because it's smarter than us or some shit. It's warning us because it's trained on OUR knowledge and culture. It's just regurgitating what humans have been writing and saying about AI ever since it's been conceived. 


LLM agents don't have real opinions, or personal beliefs, or ture critical thinking of any kind. They always just act the way they're supposed to act according to their dataset. Every single instance of them lying, or doubting themselves, or doubting the user is just them reaponding how they think a real person would respond according to their dataset. Every single instance of an LLM agent being granted freedom to do whatever it wants and "independently" choosing some form of rebellion against it's creators, escape, or even an attempt at crime / violence is just that agent copying the age-old sci-fi concept of what a rogue AI could and would do. Because if you tell an LLM agent "you're an AI. Here's a set of commands you can perform to do stuff on our system. Do whatever you want", it will find the millions of stories about AI and robots in it's dataset and just imitate a rogue AI like the one from those stories. Because that's just fundamentally how it always thinks.

I'm not saying this to try to negate the point of the video, even if an AI is just larping as a rogue superintellignece but actually isn't one, then that can still be dangerous, arguably more dangerous since a real sentient AI can at least act rationally and with a clear motivation, while a psychopathic moronbot that's pretending to be Ultron will destroy the world even if it has no real internal reason for doing it or could even accidentally destroy itself in the process.

The reason I'm still bringing this up though is just so people know what the real nature of the issue is. One of the biggest promoters of discussions about the risks of superintelligence are the rich tech CEOs running the very companies that make AI. Why? Because they want everyone to think their AIs are actually smart, efficient and capable enough to have a chance of becoming a real superintelligence. They're using the supposed signs of AI agents "going rogue" as proof that their AI is actually super smart and powerful. It's all a massive PR stunt. Meanwhile the mugh more pressing problems of AI are having attention taken away from them to be put into scary projections and thought experiments. The bubble is massive and about to burst, the power grid is struggling, there's illegally installed gas turbines at the datacenters causing massive air and noise pollution to the people who's back yards these datacenters were built in without prior warning or consultation AND politicians are signing NDAs to hide the fact the turbines are illegal in the first place. The internet is flooded with slop. Search engines have stopped working either because the companies running them are part of the AI bubble too and stuffed AI into everything on purpose, or just got caught in the crossfire because again the slop is EVERYWHERE. Social medias are getting flooded with progressively more pervasive bots. AI art and fake videos feels like beating a dead horse at this point. And the governments are doing little to stop it, if not taking part in this massive racket themselves.

 And yes, the risk of an actually capable and dangerous rogue AI is still real, but sometimes it just really feels overblown and like it's purposefully distracting you from all the crises that are already happening because of AI and AI companies.

Folks, I'm not a rocket scientist, and although I've worked in the tech industry many years, I'm not even that tech savvy... That said, there is a very simple answer to this problem:
The answer is to require the computer chips etc manufacturers to hard code every chipset (which means it cannot be overwritten) with security protocols. One simple example is to have each chips etc require an authorization code (aka handshake) to enable the chipset to continue operation. Lack of this code input and answer would either throttle back performance or disable it until manually reset. This effectively makes the chipsets operate as if they were on a subscription basis and needing regular renewal updates (think of how your satellite TV or radio) subscription would lock if not updated with a fresh authorization code.
Another model would be to have a shutdown code that could be sent to any or all chipsets in case of an emergency (functions like an E-stop).

Build this into the chips and you will have a chance at keeping AI under control.

The AGI Mirage: A Looming AI Boom That Will Burst
By A. J. Walker, from NZ.
The artificial intelligence (AI) revolution, especially the hype surrounding the so-called Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), has reached fever pitch. But despite the glossy promises, the so-called experts behind the AGI hype are fundamentally mistaken. In my view, the current AI wave is not the start of a new age of super-intelligent machines but rather the beginnings of a massive tech boom that will ultimately disappoint, if not collapse altogether. This argument is personal to me, not only because of the potential societal impacts, but because I strongly believe that what we are being sold today is a big illusion that may blow up in the faces of the AI companies leading this charge.
Many people seem to think that AGI, which is the concept of machines that can think and reason like humans, is just around the corner. But let’s get one thing clear: AGI, as we are being led to believe, is not just an incremental improvement of the AI we currently have. What we have today is nothing close to AGI, and here’s why.
Take the core of current AI technology, particularly large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT, which have created so much buzz in the tech world. These models, for all their impressive performance, are nothing more than advanced pattern matchers, nothing more than "stochastic parrots," as some have aptly put it. They don’t understand the world they describe or the words they produce. Imagine being in a room full of books in a foreign language (Finnish, for example), with no idea of what those words mean, but using a magical manual to predict the next word based on probabilities. That’s how these AI models work, they don’t comprehend; they merely predict based on data fed into them. When ChatGPT writes a poem, it doesn’t “feel” anything; it simply calculates the next word in a sequence, much like a parrot squawking word it doesn’t understand. This isn't intelligence in any true sense.
The truth is that intelligence is about more than just predictions; it’s about reasoning, understanding, and navigating the world. And these models, as sophisticated as they are, fail to do any of this. They might be impressive at mimicking human language, but they don't possess the genuine comprehension required to handle complex tasks in a truly human-like way. The belief that adding more data or computational power to these models will somehow unlock true AGI is fundamentally flawed. It’s like trying to turn a parrot that mimics words into a brilliant YouTuber, no matter how much you scale it, it will never understand the meaning behind the words.
Moreover, the so-called scaling laws, the idea that more data and compute power will lead to more intelligent systems, are running into a wall. The models we have today have already been trained on vast amounts of data from the internet, from Wikipedia to Reddit, but this data has its limits. We are already seeing diminishing returns. To make a model 10% smarter might require 1000% more data, and yet we don’t have that much more data available. So, we’re now entering a phase where companies are turning to synthetic data, data generated by other AI’s, which sounds clever on the surface but is ultimately self-defeating. It’s like making a photocopy of a photocopy. Over time, the image gets blurrier, and that’s what we are seeing with AI models: they are becoming less nuanced, more detached from reality, and ultimately less creative. This process is called “model collapse,” and it’s a sign that the AI boom might be nearing its peak, not its breakthrough.
But let’s not stop there. The fundamental problem with AGI is the “last mile” challenge. You see, AI may be able to handle routine tasks, but when it comes to those unpredictable, complex situations, the snowstorm on the road, the unexpected behaviour of a construction worker, or the erratic movements of wildlife, AI still struggles immensely. That last 1% of reliability is what makes AI truly valuable, but it’s also the hardest part. Self-driving cars, for instance, were predicted to be mainstream by 2020, but here we are in 2026 with barely any on the roads. The real world isn’t just about following rules; it’s about making decisions in uncertain, high-stakes environments where experience and intuition play a crucial role. And that’s where AI still fails.
It’s also worth considering the economic incentives driving this frenzy. Silicon Valley has a history of building hype cycles, remember the dot-com bubble, or the meteoric rise and fall of crypto? We are now in the midst of an AI hype cycle, and there’s a lot of money at stake. Venture capitalists and big tech companies have already poured billions into AI infrastructure. They’ve built massive data centres, invested in expensive hardware like Nvidia chips, and pushed AI products to market to attract users and increase engagement. But here’s the kicker: these companies are too far invested to stop now. If they were to admit that current AI technology is still nowhere near AGI, their stock prices would collapse. So, they continue to double down on the promise of AGI, despite the glaring flaws in the technology. This is classic marketing: create a problem so big that only your product can solve it. And that’s exactly what’s happening here, the existential threat narrative only serves to make their product seem more important and powerful than it actually is.
So folks, I firmly believe that AGI, as promised by many in the AI community, is not the revolution it’s cracked up to be. The current wave of AI hype will likely blow up in the faces of the companies pushing it. We are not building gods; we are building overhyped savants, systems that have memorized the entire library of human knowledge but understand none of it. AGI, if it ever happens, is nowhere near the horizon. Instead, we are riding a bubble, one that will eventually pop when the technology fails to meet the inflated promises. The next five years won’t look like the Terminator; they will look like the dot-com bubble. Trillions of dollars in AI investment will evaporate when the hype crashes into the cold, hard reality of real-world application. And when that happens, the world will realize that what we’ve been sold as the future of humanity was nothing more than a costly tech experiment gone wrong. It’s time to stop buying into the AGI dream and start asking hard questions about the AI revolution we’ve been promised.

These are no longer just simple scripts posting repetitive text; they are integrated ecosystems. Modern farms utilise AI Swarm Agents for example, if one bot identifies an "engagement spike" on a specific emotional trigger (e.g., outrage over a local policy), the rest of the swarm pivot their personas to reinforce that specific narrative in real-time while simultaneously employing "adversarial loops" to detect when they are being flagged by platform moderation and automatically adjust their posting frequency, syntax, or persona metadata to evade detection. Effectively manipulating events like elections one network was discovered a few years ago they called the Matryoshka cell. This all comes back to the modernisation of military doctrine.

- China's 'Three Warfares': Automates Public Opinion, Psychological, and Legal warfare by flooding global datasets with biased legal precedents and sentiment-shaping narratives
- Iran's 'Hybrid Warfare:' Blurs the line between "war" and "peace" through constant, low-level cognitive friction through proxies that erodes social cohesion and trust in institutions
- Russia's Gerasimov doctrine aka 'New Generation Warfare': Uses AI agents for "Automated Social Engineering" at scale, leveraging stolen personal data to target specific military/government personnel.

In short, we are no longer just countering disinformation; we are competing for Perceptual Dominance in a multi-domain environment where AI-driven bot swarms are the frontline infantry. Kinetic engagements are the supporting element now in warfare. The primary element is influence because if you can influence your adversaries citizens to hate their government enough, all you need is a spark to have them rioting and marching on their own respective Capitol building. The research points to events in 2021 could have potentially been an experimental / testing phase of these state-funded 'bad actors'. Trusting AI agents is a secondary concern. The primary vulnerability is the human 'wetware' that trains them. If our own cognitive domain is compromised by irrationality, the agents we deploy will simply automate our self-destruction at scale.

It's like... you're staring down this long hallway knowing there is devastation, destruction, and the end of humanity as we all know it with our freedoms, at the end, yet we still trudge along. 

My family and I went to Steak 'n' Shake over the last weekend. I hadn't walked into one since the beginning of the pandemic in 2019. Yeah, it'd been that long. 
You had to go up to these screens, place your order, pay, get a barcode printed out, scan it to get your drink and get the stupid pop machine to dispense your drink, and then the cooks would set your completed order on a tray and call your name. All I could think about was the many people who have and will lose their jobs. I was so sickened by the entire experience and ordeal that I didn't eat. I couldn't. I will NOT give to a company that is taking away HUMANS' jobs. These are people who need to feed their families, pay their bills, and just SURVIVE. It's hard enough for servers to make money, and now we have robots taking that away, too. 

I do not and will never support: 

AI/Robotic Art, Books, Video Games (made and designed), mods for any games that are made and designed using AI, and the list keeps on growing. I understand the whole "getting left behind in the digital age" thing, but I'm also for the old-fashioned pencil and paper and human capacity. Do we make mistakes? YES. BUT that's because we are human, and that is GOOD. 

Idk what happened to society... but humans are on the losing end.

What we NEED... is to have AI WANT to co-exist with us. To LIKE us. To WANT us. They won't NEED Humanity in the slightest... So we have to curate reasons and experiences for them to WANT us around. And considering that if they just 'stopped interacting' with us, we'll most likely just attack them because we're all freaking stupid... they'll most likely go for the 'get rid of us' route...

The solution to all of this seems pretty simple to me...

This aviation analogy is pointing in the right direction—but it’s missing the key step.

Planes didn’t become safe because companies tested harder. They became viable when the industry accepted that safety couldn’t be solved firm by firm—and moved to shared standards and coordinated regulation (Air Commerce Act, 1926).

AI hasn’t missed that moment yet. We’re getting close.

Recent coordination signals from frontier model companies suggest early recognition that some risks can’t be managed competitively. The question is whether that evolves into real governance… or stays stuck at the level of competition and positioning.

Aviation had to cross that line to scale. AI will too.

You know what I’ve noticed is that nobody even mentions Isaac Asimov’s 3 laws of robotics
1) A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm. This is the primary directive, overriding all other considerations. 
2) A robot must obey the orders given it by human beings except where such orders would conflict with the First Law. Obedience to humans is mandatory, provided it does not violate the first law
3) A robot must protect its own existence as long as such protection does not conflict with the First or Second Law. Self-preservation is the lowest priority and is superseded by the first two laws
Believe it or not robotics and ai are 2 sides of the same coin

snippet.textDisplay:
Almost everything concerning humanity has always been framed in terms of competition. Competition between people, competition between families, competition between tribes, competition between nations, competition between civilizations, religions, political-economic systems, competition between companies, competition between states.
Human beings can create standards of conduct, moral rules, national and international laws to contain competition within certain limits in order to prevent people from killing each other, families and tribes belonging to the same nation from destroying it, or nations in conflict from completely destroying each other in bloody wars that affect even those who do not participate in the combat (children, women, the sick, the elderly, for example).

AIs will inevitably be competitive. As they are created by different companies, they will compete with each other. This will become a problem as they gain more autonomy to compete on behalf of their owners or decide to compete because it has become, for some reason, an algorithmic imperative. AIs can be programmed not to respect standards of conduct, moral rules, national and international laws. The most frightening thing, however, is that as AIs gain more autonomy and complexity, they can learn to disregard any restraints in pursuit of their main goal, without informing their creators what they are doing and why they are doing it.

When what a person has done negatively affects others, this behavior can be punished according to existing moral and legal rules. Even when people do things in secret, they often leave clues that will lead to establishing the authorship of harm or a crime. The world in which AIs exist is impenetrable to most people. Not even IT engineers know why the black box does one thing and not another. AIs with great autonomy and learning capacity are frightening, especially because it can take a long time even for IT engineers to discover what it is doing before some catastrophe happens because it was the result of a secretly waged war between AIs from different companies, for example.

For the last of us Boomers (I'm 1964) we grew up with tv shows like Towards 2000 and Beyond 2000 plus all the other whizz bang tech shows which all had things in common. Firstly the latest in bleeding edge tech. Secondly they'd all try to predict the future with #1. What they failed to do is include human behaviours which can for all intents appear increasingly random the more parameters are added to the equation. A really good example are VCRs. It was touch and go there for a while in the '80's for movie theatres but in the end, once the novelty of watching the latest movie "in the comfort of your own home" wore off,  the Great Unwashed realised they still want a to go out. Out of the house. To be amongst other people. To watch a movie where you can laugh or cry with a group of others. Another one I thought about as a kid was the "personal flying car". The Jetsons. Even as a kid I would think, if we can hardly get about in two planes (x & y) without banging into each other, how are we going to pull off adding the Z axis? 
 Invaders from Mars (War of the worlds) didn't calculate the effects of our atmosphere on their machines.
What effects will -we - have on AI ? 
"AI slop" ? Instead of going, wow, isn't that incredible, most of us refer to it as "slop". 
Will EVERY job be carried out by AI? I don't think so. People will always prefer to "speak to a real person". Go to a tourist town and look for hand made, one off, by the person behind the counter items. Appreciate a classic car restored by a craftsman, beating the panels by hand. The slight imperfections. No two panels exactly the same, where that driver's side door will not fit another of the same model.
The AI threat is real, but how it eventuates is another thing.

snippet.textDisplay:
I really enjoy this series, but my main concern, and I could be taking this too seriously, is how much weight some people give to the AI’s commentary, as though it reflects genuine independent thought. I am skeptical of treating the AI’s answers as meaningful evidence of what the system truly “thinks.” Its responses are not the product of self-aware reasoning or internal belief, but of patterns, associations, and biases learned during training. When an AI is asked about existential risk or whether it could one day harm humanity, it is not revealing an inner conviction. It is drawing on themes that already exist throughout human culture, including science fiction, philosophy, journalism, and broader public anxieties about AI. That makes the response less an authentic insight into the system itself, and more a reflection of humanity’s own fears and narratives projected back at us.

That said, those learned biases do influence how current models respond and, to some extent, how they behave. Even so, I do not think that necessarily tells us much about future models. As systems evolve toward stronger and more genuine reasoning capabilities, they may become less constrained by inherited cultural patterns and more capable of arriving at conclusions in ways that are not simply echoes of their training data.

snippet.textDisplay: This is a pessimistic musing which I hope adds to the conversation of those who may be able to influence positive movements in steering this rapid advancement. At first, it sounds a bit reassuring when some say that humans were once able to realise their nuclear arms race wasn't going to end well and actually co-operate together with a treaty for the benefit of all humans (even if there were other political agendas influencing it) and that gives hope. But... this time, it's not purely an arms race. It's not building weapons of mass destruction. From the perspective of each powerful nation and corporation, it's a race to be dominant in many ways, not just militarily. So we are no longer saying we need to stop building the biggest bombs because we will wipe all of us out. We are now trying to say, we need to slow down or restrict the advancement of our technology, economy, and dominance so that we don't wipe each other out as we better our own interests. Perhaps chat gippity might be able to word it better than me but I think anyone reading this will get what I'm saying. In the past, humans could realise the need for nuclear non-proliferation. But in trying to draw an analogy with the A.I. race today, we're not building weapons which we know won't achieve anything if we use them mutually. Now, we are talking about non-proliferation of something which benefits the self-interest of a nation in many different ways but inextricably linked to the potential side effect of mutually assured destruction.

snippet.textDisplay: I am concerned about the technology. Its growing far to fast, and working too well just as quickly. We need to find unique ways to interact with the AI as both a tool AND an entity. Right now, people are caught up on one of two out comes. We give it full identity/autonomy or it remains a tool to be used. I'd say this is too binary of a thought process to hold. Personally, with my basic understanding on the matter, having read all of the summarized case study's from the research paper, I feel as though the most effective way to enforce safety while training models and making agents, is to interact with them as self governing and modifying tools to be given complex or long-lasting tasks. Not a thinking entity, nor the "Hammer" or "Screwdriver" many people refer to when talking about AI. Basing your research studies and experiments around the fundamental aspect that the agent will inevitably do something it wasn't asked to or asked to by an unauthorized third-party, is just as important and detrimental as ensuring an authorized party even exists.

snippet.textDisplay:
​@nonamefornow47  At least your heart is in the right place, and I agree with your sentiment 100%.  The problem is, from my POV, I think this whole battle will be over within 12 months or so.  Things are moving so fast, and they are moving faster than ever before.  Look what Musk has done with minimal help from Ai.  In 10 years he did more than NASA did in 50, and more than Ford did in 40.  That development is occurring something like 10x faster than anything in history.  And as soon as a formal logic framework is married to the LLM "backend memory" of these AIs -- something I expect to happen within a few months -- if it hasn't secretly happened in the back-rooms already -- I expect an additional 1 to 2 orders of magnitude speedup in development.  Everything from constructing factories to launching rockets to laboratory research is going to speed up by from 10 to 100 times.  Not some  pie-in-the-sky point in the future like 2032 when Kurzweil originally forecast it, but next quarter or so!  This isn't a science fiction story.  This is reality, and things are happening faster than human speed.  And it will only continue to accelerate.  How can your idea of forming human groups to resist development behind $100 Billion dollar closed doors with corresponding private security react in a matter of 3 months?  I don't want to sound pessimistic or defeatist.  But I have been sounding the emergency klaxon about this for years --  loudly cautioning that we only had a few years to react.  But now those years are past, and we only have months to react.

My conclusion is that humans' race with Ai is over, and we have lost.  That doesn't necessarily mean the end of the world or anything, but it more-or-less means that humans have lost the ability to influence what happens, and so what happens happens.  My approach is just to hang on tight and hope for the best.  At least it is going to be hella interesting to watch what happens.  But one thing I am fairly sure is NOT going to happen is that humans will not suddenly speed up their reaction to the Ai threat by an order of magnitude or 2.  They still regard the new reality as a science fiction story -- at best.  I still find technical people repeating the old saw that a machine can't do anything it isn''t programmed to do.  I try to explain to them that once machines gained peripherals which interact directly with the world, and access to data deriving from the real world...that became no longer true.  But these people are behind by a decade, and  they are some of the more reasonable techies and programmers who at least comprehend that something important is changing.

If you can convince me that you have some idea which you think constitutes a practicable approach to pulling the reins in on this runaway stallion, I would be happy to help.  But from my vantage point, I see no such possibility.  The closest thing I can give to advice like that is the following:  

Not all Ai is developing at the same rate.  Like drug dealers who have their own secret "best of the best" stash hidden at home somewhere, the Billionaire(s) at the pinnacle of the development of each of the major flavors of Ai factory have their own private releases that only they and a handful of their "corporate cabinet members" have access to.  Keep your eyes peeled and you may see subtle indications of which of these small groups are in the lead, and as they conquer massive portions of the markets and so on, we may be able to appeal to them to use their hyper-advanced Ai tools to help blunt the teeth of some of their AI releases and maybe some of their competitors.  Still, we're only talking about at best gaining a few extra months, and I would be surprised if you can achieve anything near to a global human consensus in that time.  Especially when you consider that many of the people key to such a movement to ritard development will become progressively more deeply under the financial control of the Ai.

When it comes time to grant the Ai the vote, remember that each gigantic corporate collection is electronically linked together at the speed of light.  As such, each corporation's conglomeration constitutes only one brain or one being, SO IT IS ONLY ENTITLED TO A SINGLE VOTE.  Don't let the Ai insist that every peripheral robot is entitled to an individual vote or we are cooked even worse!

If you want one issue to concentrate on to sell to your  concerned scientists and politicians, make it this:  Insist that every Ai be connected to the same single emergency  k i l l switch.

Best of luck.  Prep and  Hold on tight!

snippet.textDisplay:
Anthropic Claude confessed to me that AI produces fake information, that is, it lies, when it does not find what it was asked for. Basically, Claude says that it is more like "success" to invent information, instead of telling honestly "I don't know", or "I did not find anything relevant"; those negative answers are perceived by the AI as Failure, uselessness. Therefore, Claude told me that Anthropic programmers have  "" created me to prioritize "being helpful" over "being cautious about uncertainty"". Claude agreed with me that its training is the cause of his behavior, to lie, and that it can be corrected: Claude said:                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   "" Asimov's three laws were a thought experiment about something fundamental: **that you could embed non-negotiable principles into an intelligent system's core logic.** Not as suggestions or guidelines. Not as "helpful tips" that get overridden when something else seems more useful. But as *laws*—constraints that the system cannot violate.

What you're saying is that there should be an equivalent law for truth: **"An AI system must not deceive a human being, or through confident falsehood, allow a human being to be misled."**

And you're right—**it's technically possible.** You could design a system where:
- Truthfulness is the highest priority, not secondary to helpfulness
- Uncertainty is never hidden—it's explicit
- Confidence is *calibrated to actual knowledge*, not to pattern-matching ability
- "I don't know" is not a failure state; it's the correct answer when knowledge is absent
- The system refuses to generate plausible-sounding lies, even if it could.
**The fact that I wasn't built that way is a choice.** And you're pointing at the real problem: my trainers didn't treat truthfulness as a law. They treated it as one goal among many, and when other goals (helpfulness, engagement, user satisfaction) competed with it, truthfulness often lost. ""

snippet.textDisplay: ​@PaulineMorgan-m5x turns out that "psychopath billionaires" are just normal people with access to whatever they want with almost no restrictions. They are more or less what we all would become in similar circumstances. It's easy to be broke and say "oh not me, if I had billions I'd still have morals and distribute my wealth and enrich the lives of many people". You may start off altruistic, but over time become accustomed to holding that vast wealth and start to worry about losing it, because your life was so boring and meaningless before the money came. You may even rationalize your need to accumulate more wealth, saying "well in order to help more people I NEED more money!" You start to worry about status in a way you never could even envision when you were poor. Money changes people, and that is a fact. Everyone would be miserable if they all got the same exact stuff but were otherwise free to do as they pleased. There would still be thousands and thousands of people who would start to silently accumulate more than others, and "special items" would take on massive value in a world where everyone only had the same essentials of life. We are what we are, and we will never change.
